explanation: The corticobulbar tract controls lower facial muscles contralaterally. Lesion of the right corticobulbar tract causes paralysis of the left lower face (contralateral to the lesion).
keyConcept: Corticobulbar has contralateral control of lower face

explanation: The corticonuclear tract has bilateral connections with most cranial nerve nuclei, except the lower facial nucleus (which is only contralateral) and the trochlear/trigeminal motor nuclei.
keyConcept: Lower 7 facial nucleus has unilateral corticonuclear input

explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract occupies the lateral white column of the spinal cord. It is the continuation of the pyramidal decussation and controls voluntary movement of the contralateral limbs.
keyConcept: Lateral corticospinal tract in lateral white column

explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract arises mainly from the precentral gyrus (primary motor area, Brodmann area 4). Its fibers decussate in the pyramidal decussation of the medulla.
keyConcept: Lateral corticospinal arises from precentral gyrus

explanation: In the brainstem, the lateral corticospinal tract fibers are organized somatotopically with cervical fibers most lateral and sacral fibers most medial. This is the reverse of their spinal cord arrangement.
keyConcept: Sacral fibers most medial in LCST at brainstem

explanation: In the pons, the corticospinal fibers are broken into bundles by the transverse pontocerebellar fibers, creating the scattered appearance of the basis pontis.
keyConcept: Corticospinal fibers scattered in basis pontis

explanation: Motor decussation (pyramidal decussation) occurs in the caudal part of the medulla, where about 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract.
The pyramidal tract descends as a compact bundle in the medullary pyramids, not scattered. The scattering occurs only in the basis pontis due to crossing pontocerebellar fibers.
keyConcept: Pyramidal tract compact in medulla, scattered in pons

explanation: The corticospinal fibers descend as scattered bundles in the basis pontis because they are interrupted by transverse pontine fibers. This is a normal anatomical feature of the pontine base.
keyConcept: Corticospinal scattered in pons by pontine fibers

explanation: The corticobulbar tract ends on bilateral cranial nerve nuclei, not only contralateral. Some nuclei (like the lower facial) have predominantly contralateral input, but all have some bilateral contribution.
keyConcept: Corticobulbar has bilateral cranial nerve connections

explanation: This matching question tests knowledge of descending motor pathways: vestibulospinal tract extends through the whole spinal cord to facilitate anti-gravity extensors; pontine reticulospinal only reaches mid-thoracic level.
keyConcept: Vestibulospinal extends full length of cord

explanation: The cervical region of the spinal cord has the richest blood supply due to high metabolic demand and the watershed areas at C4-T1 levels, making it vulnerable to ischemic injury.
keyConcept: Cervical cord has richest blood supply

explanation: Right hemisection (Brown-Sequard): ipsilateral UMNL paralysis, ipsilateral loss of vibration/position sense, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature starting one level below. The description matches right hemisection.
Syringomyelia first affects crossing spinothalamic fibers in the central cord, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature while preserving dorsal column functions (touch, proprioception).
Positive Babinski sign (dorsiflexion of big toe with fanning) is a hallmark of upper motor neuron lesion, indicating corticospinal tract damage and release of primitive reflexes.
LMN lesion causes lost/absent tendon jerks due to direct muscle denervation, muscle atrophy, and loss of all muscle tone and reflexes.
keyConcept: LMN lesion causes lost tendon jerks

explanation: This matching tests blood supply: radicular arteries form the main supply to lumbar segments; anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior horn and lateral horn.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies anterior horn

explanation: Right hemisection at T6 causes ipsilateral paralysis and proprioception loss in the right lower limb, contralateral pain/temperature loss in the left lower limb. Fine touch from upper limb uses dorsal columns which are unaffected.
keyConcept: Hemisection spares ipsilateral upper limb fine touch

modelAnswer: The spinal cord is cylindrical but flattened anteroposteriorly. It extends from foramen magnum to lower border of L1 vertebra. It has two enlargements: cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L2-S3). It shows longitudinal fissures (anterior median fissure and posterior median sulcus) and gradual tapering at its lower end (conus medullaris).

Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina. Cervical nerves exit above their corresponding vertebra (C1-C7 exit above C1-C7). From T1-L1, nerves exit below their corresponding vertebra. The cauda equina (L2-S5) descends in the subarachnoid space before exiting through their respective foramina.

Spinal cord meninges terminate at: Dura mater ends at S2 vertebra; Arachnoid mater ends at S2 vertebra; Pia mater continues as filum terminale and ends at the dorsum of the coccyx (attached to periosteum of coccyx).

Lumbar puncture is performed to obtain CSF for diagnosis or inject medication/anesthesia. Site: between L3-L4 or L4-L5 vertebrae (just above or below L4 spine). The patient lies on side or sits forward. The needle passes through: skin, superficial fascia, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater, arachnoid mater to reach subarachnoid space (containing CSF).

Nuclei of posterior horn: (1) Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) - carries pain and temperature; (2) Nucleus proprius (laminae III, IV) - carries touch and pressure; (3) Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's column, lamina VII) - origin of spinocerebellar tracts; (4) Visceral sensory nucleus - receives visceral afferents.

Nuclei of anterior horn: (1) Medial motor nuclei - in medial column, supply muscles of neck and trunk; (2) Lateral motor nuclei - in lateral column, supply limb muscles; (a) Anterior lateral (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius); (b) Posterior lateral (flexors of forearm); (c) Postural (extensors of limb); (3) Phrenic nucleus (C3,4,5) - supplies diaphragm.

Nuclei of lateral horn: (1) Lateral horn is present from C8-L2 (sympathetic outflow) and S2-S4 (parasympathetic outflow). (2) Sympathetic lateral horn nuclei: Intermediolateral nucleus (cell column of T1-L2) - preganglionic sympathetic neurons; (3) Parasympathetic lateral horn nuclei: Sacral parasympathetic nucleus (S2-S4) - preganglionic parasympathetic neurons.

Pain pathway from face: (1st neuron) Trigeminal ganglion → (enters pons) → descends to spinal nucleus of CN V → (2nd neuron) decussates as internal arcuate fibers → ascends as trigeminal lemniscus → VPM of thalamus → (3rd neuron) via posterior limb of internal capsule → postcentral gyrus (S1 cortex).

Neurons in pain pathway from body: (1st) Dorsal root ganglion cell - peripheral process receives pain, central process enters spinal cord; (2nd) Neuron in posterior horn (substantia gelatinosa/lamina I) - axon decussates in anterior white commissure and ascends 1-2 segments; (3rd) Neuron in VPL nucleus of thalamus - axon projects to somatosensory cortex via internal capsule.
